There had been 158 incidents of restraint on Svanna ward, and 23 on Hooper ward. Of those, 7 were in the prone position on Svanna ward and none on Hooper ward. Managers told us, these related to a small patient cohort with complex needs and multiple co-morbidities, one of whom had been transferred within the 5-month data period, and another who had since been transferred to an alternative placement.

There had been 64 incidents of rapid tranquilisation on Svanna ward, and 11 on Hooper ward. There had been 6 incidents of seclusion on Svanna ward, with none on Hooper ward. The longest period for a patient being nursed in seclusion was 6 days on Svanna ward, with none on Hooper ward. All incidents of restraint, seclusion and rapid tranquilisation were reviewed at clinical governance meetings. Managers and the security lead were also able to access CCTV footage from communal areas to review incidents of restraint.

Staff used seclusion appropriately and followed best practice when they did so. At the time of our inspection, a patient was being nursed in seclusion. Staff monitored all patients for the first hour of seclusion. Details of the patient in seclusion was displayed and noted on a wipe board, including the time of previous nursing review, time of next nursing review and the items the patient took into seclusion.

We reviewed 3 seclusion records. Staff maintained appropriate records that showed that patients were afforded the appropriate checks and safeguards outlined in the Mental Health Act code of practise. We found that the current out of hours arrangements meant that the on-call doctor, who would form part of the independent reviewing team for patients nursed in seclusion, may also be the established ward doctor. This had happened recently, which meant that the make-up of the independent review team had not complied with guidance. On another occasion where an independent review was required, this had not occurred. We raised this during our inspection. The hospital manager subsequently told us that updated procedures that addressed out of hours had been introduced. The hospital manager also told us, they had added independent reviews on the ‘Hospital Safety Huddle’ template to improve oversight of this aspect of seclusion governance.

topicareas.qualityStatementscore: 2 - Evidence shows some shortfalls in the standard of care

topicareas.name: Learning culture

evidenceCategory.commentary:
The service had a proactive and positive culture of safety, based on openness and honesty. They listened to concerns about safety and investigated and reported safety events. Lessons were learnt to continually identify and embed good practice.

Staff knew what incidents to report and how to report them via an electronic incident reporting system. Staff told us that they would report any incident of harm, potential harm or risks to safety.

Staff told us incidents and never events were discussed in supervision, daily huddles, team meetings and reflective practice. Incidents were also discussed at clinical governance meetings with learning from these disseminated to each ward.

Themes and trends identified from incidents were discussed with the staff team.

Staff understood the duty of candour. They were open and transparent and gave patients and families a full explanation when things went wrong. Duty of candour incidents were reviewed and discussed at the monthly clinical governance meetings.

Staff were informed about learning through the provider’s lessons learnt newsletters. This information was shared with bank staff through group supervision

Managers debriefed and supported staff after any serious incident. Staff felt well supported and were offered the opportunity to debrief immediately following incidents and also in regular reflective practice sessions. The hospital had introduced Trauma Risk Management (TRiM), a trauma-focused peer support system designed to help staff who have experienced a traumatic, or potentially traumatic, event. Staff could also access Sustaining Resilience at Work (STRaW), a well-being peer support system. One staff member described the support they received from TRiM after being involved in an incident and told us that it had been helpful to their wellbeing.

topicareas.qualityStatementscore: 3 - Evidence shows a good standard of care

topicareas.name: Medicines optimisation

evidenceCategory.commentary:
The service made sure that medicines and treatments were safe and met patients’ needs, capacities and preferences. They involved patients in planning, including when changes happened.

At our inspection in December 2024, patients did not always receive their medicines safely and as prescribed. Some patients’ physical health was not monitored appropriately, including venous thromboembolism (VTE) assessments and following rapid tranquilisation (RT). Some patients detained under the Mental Health Act (MHA) had been administered medicines that were not in line with MHA consent to treatment authorisations. During this inspection, we found improvements. The service had strengthened medicines management. Patients received their medicines safely as prescribed. Staff regularly reviewed the effects of medicines on each patient’s mental and physical health in daily safety huddles and multidisciplinary meetings. On the day of inspection, the service was in the process of moving over to a new electronic prescribing and medicines administration (ePMA) system.

A review of care records showed that appropriate checks were carried out for patients administered rapid tranquilisation, lithium and clozapine. Medicines were administered in line with relevant Mental Health Act ‘consent to treatment’ authorisations where needed.

When PRN (‘when required’) medicines were used, the reason for administration and what else had been tried first was clearly recorded on the daily electronic care records. A review of 8 care records demonstrated evidence of physical health reviews completed on admission included VTE screening.

Two of the 3 patients we spoke with confirmed they had enough information about their medicines and side effects. Changes in their medicines was discussed and agreed with them in ward rounds. An external pharmacist from the hospitals medicine suppliers carried out weekly medicine audits. Results of the audits and any shortfalls were discussed at the clinical governance meetings.

Managers had a dedicated company card to purchase medicines if needed from the local pharmacy.

Staff regularly reviewed the effects of medicines on each patient’s mental and physical health in line with guidance from the National Institute of Health and Care Excellence (NICE).

topicareas.qualityStatementscore: 3 - Evidence shows a good standard of care

topicareas.name: Safe and effective staffing

evidenceCategory.commentary:
They worked together well to provide safe care that met people’s individual needs. Staff were suitably qualified, skilled and experienced, but compliance rates for administration of some specialist medicines needed to improve. There were some occasions where safe staffing levels had not been achieved and measures had been taken promptly to ensure people were kept safe.

Overall, the service had enough staff with the right qualifications, skills, training and experience to keep people safe from avoidable harm and abuse and to provide the right care and treatment.

Managers calculated and reviewed the number and grade of nurses, nursing assistants and healthcare assistants for each shift. The service used a staffing matrix which determined the numbers of staff required, dependent on the number of patients and their acuity.

Ward managers could adjust staffing levels daily in accordance with the needs of patients. Where bank and agency were used, those staff received an induction and were familiar with the wards.

At the time of our inspection both wards were fully established with additional over recruitment to some roles. The average staff turnover rate across the hospital was 3% in the 3 months leading up to our inspection. The average sickness rate was 2.8% within the same 3 month period.

Staffing records for Hooper ward showed that, over a six-day period in May 2026, staffing fell below minimum safe levels. This was escalated immediately, with action taken to ensure safety including, review of leave, postponed activities, and closing the ward to admissions. Staffing levels in the 3 months preceding were within the hospital’s safe staffing matrix range.

The name of the primary and associate nurse was displayed outside each patient’s room. Patients told us they had regular one-to-one time with their named nurse most of the time, when that could not happen, staff informed them. All patients we spoke with said support was available when needed. Two of 3 patients we spoke with said at times there was not enough staff; one told us this was when they were lots of one-to-one observations happening.

Staff shortages rarely resulted in staff cancelling escorted leave or ward activities. Some staff told us, short notice cancellation of shifts did sometimes result in delays to escorted leave, and activities could be postponed. Leaders told us, late shift cancellations had been recognised as a challenge, and they were working with staff, with measures in place to reduce the occurrence.

On Hooper and Svanna wards, there was enough staff on each shift to carry out any physical interventions safely, and where needed, additional staff were deployed. The hospital had appointed a Prevention and Management of Violence and Aggression (PMVA) lead who delivered training to new staff.

There was appropriate medical cover day and night and a doctor could attend the ward quickly in an emergency. Patients were seen and monitored in a timely way. The service operated an on-call system out of hours.

At our inspection in December 2024, the provider had not ensured that all eligible staff completed mandatory training appropriate for their role to meet the needs of the patients. During this inspection we saw improvements. Overall compliance for mandatory training was 98% for Svanna Ward and 91% Hooper Ward. However, we found that 66% of staff had completed mandatory training to administer buccal midazolam. We raised this with the hospital manager. They took immediate action to ensure that a member of staff was on duty for each shift who could administer this medication across all wards. Subsequently additional training was provided to increase compliance with this course. We also saw that 25% of staff on Svanna Ward had completed mandatory training in complaints. We raised this with the hospital manager. They subsequently told us that additional training had been arranged and compliance with complaints training for Svanna Ward had risen in excess of 92%.

topicareas.qualityStatementscore: 2 - Evidence shows some shortfalls in the standard of care

topicareas.name: Safe environments

evidenceCategory.commentary:
The service detected and controlled potential risks in the care environment. They made sure equipment, facilities and technology supported the delivery of safe care.

Staff completed regular risk assessments of the care environment, both on Hooper and Svanna wards. Staff carried out health and safety checks of the wards and reviewed all environment checks in daily oversight meetings.

The layout of both Hooper and Svanna wards allowed staff to observe all parts of the wards, with mitigations in place for the blind spots including mirrors and closed-circuit television (CCTV).

Staff knew about ligature risks on the wards and could describe how these were being mitigated. Ligature risks were addressed as part of staff induction and ongoing training. An annual ligature risk assessment had been completed, reviewed and updated 3 weeks prior to our inspection.

There was no mixed sex accommodation

Staff had easy access to alarms and patients had easy access to nurse call systems in their bedrooms. Staff on Hooper and Svanna wards carried out weekly checks of patient call alarms. Staff told us personal alarms worked well and were checked daily.

The seclusion room allowed clear observation and two-way communication, and temperature control was in place. It had toilet facilities and a visible clock. There was no seclusion garden, but patients could be escorted into the garden for fresh air.

The clinic rooms were fully equipped, with accessible resuscitation equipment and emergency drugs that staff checked daily. The clinic rooms were visibly clean and tidy. At our inspection in December 2024, weekly calibration records for blood glucose monitoring machines on both wards were not up to date. During this inspection we saw improvements. Blood glucose and ketone monitoring machine checks were completed weekly.

topicareas.qualityStatementscore: 3 - Evidence shows a good standard of care

topicareas.name: Safe systems, pathways and transitions

evidenceCategory.commentary:
The service worked with people and healthcare partners to establish and maintain safe systems of care, in which safety was managed or monitored. Some people were placed a long way from where they lived and some people experienced delayed discharge while suitable move on placements were identified.

Staff had easy access to clinical information, and it was easy for them to maintain high quality clinical paper-based and electronic records. Patient notes were comprehensive, and all staff could access them easily. Records were stored securely.

The service’s referral and admission processes ensured that all essential information about a new patient was available to determine if the patients’ needs could be safely and appropriately met. At the time of our inspection, patients on the wards were placed out of area from where they lived. Whilst some patients were from South London, the majority were from farther afield, including Devon and Wales. This impacted upon some patient’s ability to maintain regular, face to face contact with their families and other people who were important to them. One carer reported, due to the distance of the hospital, there could not visit they relative as often as they would like.

The service experienced delays to discharge whilst the placing authority identified appropriate move on placements. During the inspection 2 patients on Hooper Ward and 1 patient Svanna Ward were experiencing delayed discharge. We discussed with managers the delayed discharge of 1 patient whose needs the hospital had identified it could no longer safely or appropriately meet. Managers told us, actions had been taken to escalate concerns, and we were notified shortly after the inspection that this patient had transferred to a suitable placement.

topicareas.qualityStatementscore: 2 - Evidence shows some shortfalls in the standard of care

topicareas.name: Safeguarding

evidenceCategory.commentary:
The service worked with patients and healthcare partners to understand what being safe meant to them and the best way to achieve that. They concentrated on improving patients’ lives while protecting their right to live in safety, free from bullying, harassment, abuse, discrimination, avoidable harm and neglect. The service shared safeguarding concerns quickly and appropriately.

Staff knew how to recognise adults and children at risk of or suffering, significant harm and worked in partnership with other agencies to protect them. Staff we spoke with knew who the safeguarding lead was and felt confident in reporting safeguarding concerns.

Staff received training on how to recognise and report abuse. All new staff received safeguarding training during induction, with ongoing mandatory refresher training provided in accordance with their role and responsibilities. Patients we spoke with said they felt safe on the ward.

Staff followed safe procedures for children visiting the hospital. The hospital had a designated room for visitors with children off the ward.

Safeguarding was discussed in various forums, including a weekly site safeguarding meeting attended by senior managers. This meeting reviewed safeguarding concerns, actions, and emerging risks. A central safeguarding team had oversight and completed audits in relation to safeguarding actions.

topicareas.qualityStatementscore: 3 - Evidence shows a good standard of care

keyQuestionRatings.name: Well-led
keyQuestionRatings.commentary:
This means we looked for evidence that service leadership, management and governance assured high-quality, person-centred care; supported learning and innovation; and promoted an open, fair culture.

At our last assessment we rated this key question requires improvement. At this assessment the rating has improved to good. The service had made tangible improvements in its governance systems and was no longer in breach of regulations.

This meant the service was consistently managed and well-led. Leaders and the culture they created promoted high-quality, person-centred care.

topicareas.name: Capable, compassionate and inclusive leaders

evidenceCategory.commentary:
The service had inclusive leaders at all levels who understood the context in which they delivered care, treatment and support and embodied the culture and values of their workforce and organisation. Leaders had the skills, knowledge, experience and credibility to lead effectively. They did so with integrity, openness and honesty.

Leaders had the skills, knowledge and experience to perform their roles. The registered manager had been in the post since June 2025. The registered manager was a registered nurse. They had experience of working in forensic, rehabilitation and acute settings.

Leaders had a good understanding of the services they managed. They could explain clearly how the teams were working to provide high-quality care. During our inspection the registered manager demonstrated a good understanding of patients, the staff team and matters relating to the provision of acute and psychiatric intensive care services.

Leaders were visible in the service and approachable for patients and staff. Staff we spoke with told us leaders were visible in the service and felt they could raise any concerns they had to them. They reported, an open, transparent, and supportive culture between colleagues and the leadership team. For example, one staff member told us about the support they received from their manager and colleagues after an incident they were involved in.

Leadership development opportunities were available, including opportunities for staff below team manager level. Some leaders previously worked for the service in other roles before progressing to their current positions.

topicareas.qualityStatementscore: 3 - Evidence shows a good standard of care

topicareas.name: Freedom to speak up

evidenceCategory.commentary:
The service fostered a positive culture where people felt they could speak up and their voice would be heard.

Staff supported, informed, and involved families or carers as appropriate. The hospital held Family and Friends meetings bi-monthly, which could be attended in person or online. The hospital also distributed a bi-monthly newsletter to family and carers. This provided updates on the hospital, how families and carers could be involved, and past and forthcoming events.

Staff provided carers with information about how to access a carer’s assessment.

Staff received regular updates of the provider's work through the ‘MyCygnet’ intranet, newsletters, emails, social media, and team meetings. The provider also used its website and social media to keep the public informed of the work they were undertaking to support patients, families, and carers.

The service engaged well with patients, carers, and staff to help them plan and manage the way the service operated. Staff surveys were completed, results analysed and action plans created based on the results.

Feedback was encouraged, and people were supported to provide it in ways that best suited them. Patients feedback through weekly community meetings, patient forums, patient council meetings, and their local advocacy services.

topicareas.qualityStatementscore: 3 - Evidence shows a good standard of care

topicareas.name: Governance, management and sustainability

evidenceCategory.commentary:
The service had clear responsibilities, roles, systems of accountability and good governance. They used these to manage and deliver good quality, sustainable care, treatment and support. They act on the best information about risk, performance and outcomes, and share this securely with others when appropriate.

Our findings from the other key questions demonstrated that governance processes operated effectively at team level and that performance and risk were managed well.

Since the last inspection, the service had made significant improvements in governance and oversight. All areas relating to governance, risk, and performance monitoring had been strengthened. As a result, the service was no longer in breach of regulation.

Governance and performance monitoring arrangements were in place to support service delivery, identify risks, and monitor the quality and safety of care. There were systems and procedures to ensure that wards were safe and clean. Staffing levels were sufficient to meet patients' assessed needs safely, with additional staff rostered if required. Staff were trained, supervised, and appraised appropriately. Staff ensured patient outcomes and clinical effectiveness.

The registered manager and senior leadership team were aware of areas where improvement could be made and were committed to improving care and treatment for patients. They recognised improvements in the service needed to be embedded and sustained.

There was a clear framework of communication ensured staff were kept updated on the service, incidents, safeguarding, complaints and essential information though regular clinical governance, and daily huddle meetings.

Leaders had established appropriate policies, procedures, and activities to ensure safety and effectiveness. Regular audits were carried out, with action plans developed where shortfalls identified.

The service maintained a risk register and staff could escalate concerns when required. Staff concerns matched those on the risk register. The service had an up-to-date business continuity plan which details actions in emergencies to maintain the service.

topicareas.qualityStatementscore: 3 - Evidence shows a good standard of care

topicareas.name: Learning, improvement and innovation

evidenceCategory.commentary:
The service focused on continuous learning, innovation and improvement across the organisation and local system. They encouraged creative ways of delivering equality of experience, outcome and quality of life for patients. They actively contributed to safe, effective practice and research.

The service was making improvements to its systems. On the day of our inspection, the hospital was in the process of moving over to a new electronic prescribing and medicines administration (ePMA) system.

The hospital had recently moved to a risk formulation model. Staff had received training and it was embedded as business-as-usual approach, and staff informed us, it would be disseminated across other Cygnet locations.

The hospital had several quality improvement initiatives and a research project was in progress, where staff had the opportunity to participate and apply them. The service was accredited through the Enabling Environments framework, a Royal College of Psychiatrists’ initiative focused on improving the quality of relationships and culture within services. The whole hospital had achieved accreditation with Triangle of Care, a quality improvement scheme aimed at improving support for carers. A Quality Network for Psychiatric Intensive Care Units (QNPICU) accreditation process was underway for Svanna Ward, whilst a Quality Network for Working-age inpatient wards (QNWA) accreditation process was in train for Hooper ward.

Over the few months preceding our visit, the OT team had led a ‘Creative Projects Group’ and created a Discharge Tree. The idea being that when a patient was discharged, they write a short message on a paper leaf, to then be stuck on the tree. The tree was displayed for other patients to see these messages and provide hope and motivation for their own recovery.

topicareas.qualityStatementscore: 3 - Evidence shows a good standard of care

topicareas.name: Partnerships and communities

evidenceCategory.commentary:
The service understood their duty to collaborate and work in partnership, so services work seamlessly for people. They share information and learning with partners and collaborate for improvement.

Staff worked in partnership with other professionals to ensure patients received holistic care and treatment which met their needs.

Patients could meet with members of the provider’s senior leadership team and commissioners to share their feedback and experiences.

The People’s Council was a co-produced forum within Cygnet Health Care to give a voice to patient, residents and family carers at every level of the organisation, held monthly. The meetings promoted discussions on how services could make quality improvements as well as wider decisions around the service, local protocols and group policy. The People’s Council also gave the opportunity for the sharing of best practice and lessons learned across the organisation.

The provider gave commissioners regular updates on care pathways and discharge plans.

We received feedback from external partners, which was positive, and they told us about collaborative working to support patients. They told us that information was received in a timely manner.

topicareas.qualityStatementscore: 3 - Evidence shows a good standard of care

topicareas.name: Shared direction and culture

evidenceCategory.commentary:
The service had a shared vision, strategy and culture. This was based on transparency, equity, equality and human rights, diversity and inclusion, engagement, and understanding challenges and the needs of people and their communities.

Staff knew and understood the provider’s strategy, vision, and values and how they were applied in the work of their team. Staff promoted the organisation's five values of integrity, trust, empowerment, respect, and care. During the inspection, we saw these values reflected in daily practice, which centred on improving the quality-of-care patients received through, compassion, empowerment, partnership, and involvement.

Staff knew and understood the provider’s vision and values and how they were applied in the work of their team. The organisation’s five values were displayed throughout the hospital and were part of induction and mandatory training for staff.

Staff had access to equality networks, and organised events for staff and patients which celebrated diversity. There were policies in relation to equality and diversity and promoting human rights was part of mandatory training.

Staff had the opportunity to contribute to discussions about the strategy for their service, including when the service was changing. Forums included reflective practice sessions, staff meetings, quality improvement meetings, access to Freedom to Speak Up guardians, and staff surveys. Experts by experience visited the hospital weekly to provide peer support to patients, participated in people’s council meetings and contributed to improvement ideas.

For example, the hospital on-site Recovery College a co-production, run by patients and staff, provided educational courses and workshops. Patients valued the college, describing it as confidence‑building, and helping their self‑esteem.

topicareas.qualityStatementscore: 3 - Evidence shows a good standard of care

topicareas.name: Workforce equality, diversity and inclusion

evidenceCategory.commentary:
The service valued diversity in their workforce. They worked towards an inclusive and fair culture by improving equality and equity.

The service valued diversity within its workforce. Leaders actively worked to improve equality, diversity and equity for all staff. Staff had access to six equality networks, these included LGBT+, Disability Network, Women's Network, Multicultural Network, Men's Health, and Staff Carers. Each network was represented by a staff champion. Staff reported fair treatment and access to opportunities for development and progression.

Managers enabled flexible working and made reasonable adjustments to support staff in their roles. The workforce reflected a diverse background and the needs of the patient group, and the service monitored equality performance against the Workforce Race Equality Standard (WRES) and Workforce Disability Equality Standard (WDES)

topicareas.qualityStatementscore: 3 - Evidence shows a good standard of care

asgRatings.title: Ongoing Assessment for Cygnet Hospital Beckton
asgRatings.name: Personality disorder services
asgRatings.commentary:
Date of assessment: 2 to 24 June 2026.

Cygnet Hospital Beckton is a 58-bed specialist hospital for women of working age. It is based in the London Borough of Newham and is run by Cygnet Health Care Limited, an independent provider group. The hospital admits patients funded by NHS England and Integrated Care Boards.

The hospital provides acute wards and psychiatric intensive care units and personality disorder services.

This report is specific to personality disorder services, which comprise New Dawn Ward and Upping Ward. This service is for female patients with primary diagnoses of personality disorders, many of whom have complex presentations with co-occurring mental health conditions. Both wards provide care to informal patients and those detained under the Mental Health Act 1983.

New Dawn Ward is an 18-bed Tier 4 personality disorder service. Upping Ward is a 15-bed complex personality disorder unit. At the time of our inspection, New Dawn was fully occupied, and Upping Ward had 12 patients admitted.

We carried out an unannounced site visit as part of our inspection on 2-4 June 2026 and visited both wards. We previously inspected the service in December 2024 and rated it requires improvement. At that time, we identified breaches of regulations in relation to safe care and treatment, staffing and governance.

This current inspection was comprehensive and covered all key questions and quality statements. We have combined the scores for these to achieve the overall rating. Following this inspection, the overall rating has improved to good. The service was no longer in breach of regulations.

We found several areas of good practice. We found significant improvements in the areas of concern identified in our previous inspection. These included medicines management, physical health monitoring, staff training and supervision, patient access to independent advocacy and governance processes. The new managers demonstrated commitment to learning and continuous improvement. Staff described a positive and open culture with good support from managers. There was evidence of strong multidisciplinary team (MDT) working, and the wards were well-resourced with MDT staff. Patient feedback about staff was consistently positive. We saw caring interactions between staff and patients and heard about many examples of patient involvement and co-production.

We also found some areas where best practice could be improved, most of which the managers were already aware of. The needs of a small number of patients on Upping Ward exceeded those the service was able to meet safely, impacting safety and resulting in increased incidents. Managers were working to identify more suitable placements for those patients. Shortly after our visit, we heard that one patient had been successfully transferred to a more appropriate setting. Feedback about the food on offer was mixed. We were told that the service was working on improving the menu. The hospital-wide panic alarm sound was loud and went on for a long time. The alarm system was due to be replaced in July 2026, and staff expected this to improve following the upgrade. We also identified an area for improvement in record keeping related to checking ligature cutting equipment on Upping Ward and NEWS2 documentation, which we discussed with staff during our inspection.

Mental Health Act and Mental Capacity Act Compliance Summary

Mental Health Act

The service provided care to informal patients and those detained under the Mental Health Act (MHA) 1983. There was a notice to tell informal patients that they were free to leave.

Staff had a good understanding of the MHA, the Code of Practice and the guiding principles. All staff on both wards had completed training in MHA awareness. Staff had access to administrative support and legal advice on implementation of the MHA.

The care and treatment records we viewed demonstrated that when patients were detained under the MHA, staff read and explained their rights and repeated this regularly.

Patients had access to independent mental health advocacy, in line with their statutory rights. The independent advocates visited the wards regularly. Patients knew about independent advocacy and how to access it. Managers told us about implementing an opt out system for independent advocacy, with all detained patients registered for advocacy support on admission.

Staff ensured that patients were able to take Section 17 leave (permission for patients to leave hospital) when this had been granted.

Staff stored copies of patients' detention papers and associated records appropriately. Staff requested an opinion from a second opinion appointed doctor (SOAD) when necessary.

Mental Capacity Act

Staff had a good understanding of the Mental Capacity Act (MCA). On both wards, 100% of staff had completed training in the MCA and Deprivation of Liberty Safeguards.

Staff obtained and documented consent from patients appropriately.

In the care and treatment records we reviewed, staff had assessed patients’ capacity to consent on a decision-specific basis and documented the outcome appropriately.
asgRatings.narrative: The service is performing well and meeting our expectations.
asgRatings.overallPeopleExperience:
We spoke with 5 patients and 2 carers of patients across both wards. We attended 2 community meetings and with consent from patients, 2 ward rounds.

Patients and carers described staff as kind, supportive, respectful and polite. One patient said about staff: “They don’t give up on people and always want you to get better”.

Patients and carers told us that they (or their relatives) felt safe on the wards, although some reported feeling less safe during incidents involving other patients. Most patients said that staff carried out restraint safely and that debriefs were offered. Patients knew about their level of observations and the rationale for it. They did not share concerns about restrictions in place and were involved in discussions about blanket restrictions.

Patients were positive about the activities and therapy, and knew how to access independent advocacy. They felt involved in their care planning. They said staff supported their individual needs and helped them to understand and manage their own risks better. Most did not report concerns about staff availability.

However, feedback about the food on offer was less positive. Some patients were not happy with its taste or quality, and some found the menu repetitive.

In the community meetings and ward rounds we observed, patients participated in discussions openly. The community meetings were chaired by patients and well-attended by patients and staff. Patient representatives were involved in decision-making within the service.

Patients and carers knew how to complain and provide feedback to the service. The service conducted regular patient and carer surveys. The most recent surveys were completed in 2026, and their results were generally consistent with the feedback we heard. For example, some respondents wanted improvement in food and more regular updates.

keyQuestionRatings.name: Caring
keyQuestionRatings.commentary:
This means we looked for evidence that the service involved people and treated them with compassion, kindness, dignity and respect.

At our last assessment we rated this key question good. At this assessment the rating has remained good.

This meant people were supported and treated with dignity and respect; and involved as partners in their care.

topicareas.name: Independence, choice and control

evidenceCategory.commentary:
The service promoted patients’ independence, so they knew their rights and had choice and control over their own care, treatment and wellbeing.

Most patients and carers we spoke with told us they were satisfied with their level of involvement in care and access to the care plan. They said they received enough information and updates about treatment and medicines.

Staff obtained and documented consent from patients and respected their decisions in this. The care and treatment records we reviewed demonstrated that when patients were detained under the Mental Health Act (MHA), staff read and explained their rights and repeated this regularly. An informal patient we spoke with confirmed they knew they could leave the hospital. All staff on both wards had completed training in MHA awareness.

Patients told us they knew about independent advocacy. Advocates visited the wards regularly, and posters with advocacy details were displayed throughout the hospital. Managers told us about implementing an opt out system for advocacy, with all detained patients registered for advocacy support on admission.

Staff were committed to promoting patient independence and least restrictive practice. The care plans we viewed were recovery-orientated, with clear evidence of patient voice. One patient told us about the skills they had learnt to manage their condition, and another how staff supported them to improve budgeting. Patients were positive about the occupational therapy (OT) and psychology provision which they described as skills-focused. OT staff described pride in supporting patients to regain confidence and practical skills.

An expert by experience worked with patients and staff to ensure that service development was informed by patient voice. Each ward had a nominated carer champion who supported carer engagement.

topicareas.qualityStatementscore: 3 - Evidence shows a good standard of care

topicareas.name: Kindness, compassion and dignity

evidenceCategory.commentary:
The service treated patients with kindness, empathy and compassion and respected their privacy and dignity. Staff treated colleagues from other organisations with kindness and respect.

Throughout our inspection, we observed staff interacting with patients in a kind, respectful and relaxed manner. In the meetings we attended, staff demonstrated a good understanding of patients. Patients were comfortable engaging with staff, demonstrating positive therapeutic relationships.

We spoke with 5 patients, all of whom told us they found staff kind, supportive and respectful. They described staff as “lovely”, “very nice” and very supportive, including during crises. One patient said about staff: “They don’t give up on people and always want you to get better”. Another said that staff praised even their small achievements. The 2 carers we spoke with also said they found staff kind, polite and respectful. However, one patient told us that agency staff could be rude.

Patients told us that staff supported them to understand their own risks better and felt involved in their care and treatment. Patients said staff understood and supported their individual needs. Care planning was personalised, with clear evidence of patient voice in the care records we reviewed. Carers’ feedback about staff meeting their relatives’ individual needs was mostly positive. One carer said staff had a very good understanding of their relative’s needs, however another thought staff could sometimes be too busy to meet the needs of their relative.

Staff respected the confidentiality of information about patients. Staff explained and documented consent, confidentiality and information sharing.

We sought feedback from partner agencies who regularly worked with the service. One stakeholder described staff as courteous, professional and caring, and said they treated patients with kindness and compassion. Another stakeholder said that staff encouraged people to participate in discussions and share feedback.

topicareas.qualityStatementscore: 3 - Evidence shows a good standard of care

topicareas.name: Responding to people’s immediate needs

evidenceCategory.commentary:
The service listened to and understood patients’ needs, views and wishes. Staff responded to patients’ needs in the moment and acted to minimise any discomfort, concern or distress.

Staff demonstrated a good understanding of risks specific to their patient group and of patients’ individual risks. The risks, and any changes to them, were discussed daily. Staff told us about providing additional support to their bank and agency colleagues to ensure awareness of patient-specific risks and ward routines.

Patients we spoke with said that staff understood and met their individual needs. We observed staff engaging with patients and responding to their requests promptly. One patient told us how the therapeutic relationships they had built with staff, including staff taking time to speak, had contributed to their ongoing recovery. Another patient told us that staff checked on them more often to offer support when they noticed they felt low.

Some staff on Upping Ward spoke about the recent incidents linked to a small number of patients whose needs exceeded those the service could meet safely. They acknowledged the challenges in supporting these patients, and recognised the importance of knowing the patients well, preventative strategies and effective therapeutic support.

Staff were committed to using restraint only as the last resort, with support from Prevention and Management of Violence and Aggression (PMVA) leads. Most patients who had been restrained said they understood the reason for this, and that staff had restrained them safely.

topicareas.qualityStatementscore: 3 - Evidence shows a good standard of care

topicareas.name: Treating people as individuals

evidenceCategory.commentary:
The service treated people as individuals and aimed to ensure people’s care, support, and treatment met their needs and preferences. They took account of people’s strengths, abilities, aspirations, culture and unique backgrounds and protected characteristics.

Staff considered patients’ needs and preferences and documented those in the care plans. There was strong consideration of autism and learning disabilities. Staff adapted provision for individual needs, for example by using communication cards with some neurodivergent patients.

Staff we spoke with were committed to providing person-centred care, including choice of activities for different needs and interests, and identifying least restrictive practices. Staff demonstrated a good understanding of women-specific health issues, including screenings and sexual health.

Feedback from patients showed that staff met their individual needs, including cultural and spiritual needs. Two patients told us how staff supported them to attend a local church. Religious materials were available, and faith leaders visited the wards.

Patients were provided with a choice of food to meet their dietary needs, intolerances, or preferences. However, some patients were not happy with the quality or taste of the food on offer. Two patients said they found the menu repetitive. Some patients said they preferred to buy food from local shops or order takeaways. Shortly after our inspection visit, managers provided an update that the dietitian was working with patients on improving the menu. The new menu was expected to be in place within a few weeks.

There was information on display to make diverse groups of people feel welcome and included. For example, interpreter service details were clearly displayed, and a joint Pride celebration event was recently held by staff and patients.

One partner agency stakeholder said that staff took a holistic approach to patients’ individual needs, and another that staff tailored care in response to patients’ changing needs.

topicareas.qualityStatementscore: 3 - Evidence shows a good standard of care

topicareas.name: Workforce wellbeing and enablement

evidenceCategory.commentary:
The service cared about and promoted the wellbeing of their staff, and supported and enabled staff to always deliver person-centred care.

Staff we spoke with were proud and positive about working for their teams and the provider. They described a supportive culture, good teamwork and morale, and confidence in the local leadership. Staff reported feeling respected and valued. Staff received regular supervision and appraisal, the records of which demonstrated discussions of their health and wellbeing, development needs and equality, diversity and inclusion.

Staff acknowledged the recent challenges in caring for patients with high levels of emotional distress, and the emotional impact of this. Additionally, staff said this increased the administrative burden associated with incident documentation and resulted in staffing pressures. Staff however reported that managers had listened to their concerns and had taken steps to increase staffing levels, with one staff member saying: “They are not only listening but doing something about it”. Staff received support following incidents and could access additional resources. The provider’s employee assistance programme included Trauma Risk Management (TRiM), specialist support for challenging or traumatic events.

Staff had access to large comfortable staff rooms, which were well-utilised during our visit.

The provider recognised staff success, for example through staff award boards displayed throughout the hospital and the provider’s magazine which shared news across the organisation.

topicareas.qualityStatementscore: 3 - Evidence shows a good standard of care

keyQuestionRatings.name: Effective
keyQuestionRatings.commentary:
This means we looked for evidence that people’s care, treatment and support achieved good outcomes and promoted a good quality of life, based on best available evidence.

At our last assessment we rated this key question good. At this assessment the rating has remained good.

This meant people’s outcomes were consistently good, and people’s feedback confirmed this.

topicareas.name: Assessing needs

evidenceCategory.commentary:
The service made sure patients’ care and treatment was effective by assessing and reviewing their health, care, wellbeing and communication needs with them.

The service had now improved its processes to complete comprehensive mental and physical health assessments.

We viewed 8 care and treatment records. Physical health assessment on admission included choking risk assessment, venous thromboembolism (VTE) screening, and a baseline electrocardiogram (ECG). Allergies were appropriately recorded. Staff developed care plans that met the needs identified during assessment. All care plans were personalised and holistic, created with patient involvement. For example, for an autistic patient, sensory assessment had been completed and a hospital passport was in place. Where applicable, there was evidence of active carer involvement in patients’ care. All care plans had been regularly updated in ward rounds, with patient and multidisciplinary team (MDT) input. Regular one-to-one nursing sessions and ongoing medical reviews were clearly documented.

Staff monitored patients’ physical health needs daily. Following admission, physical health checks were completed annually, and referrals to GP or specialist care were completed as needed. Mobile dentists visited the wards regularly.

All eligible staff on both wards had completed mandatory training in physical health awareness and physiological observation. The hospital recently employed a new dedicated physical health lead who actively supported staff and patients. Due to an increased incidence of self-harm on the wards, the physical health lead had delivered wound care training to staff.

We spoke with 5 patients, all of whom told us they were involved in their care planning and had access to a copy of their care plan. They said their individual needs were met, although one patient said their sensory needs could be met better. In the 2 ward rounds we observed, patients contributed openly to discussions about their care. MDT demonstrated a good understanding of the patients and their needs.

topicareas.qualityStatementscore: 3 - Evidence shows a good standard of care

topicareas.name: Consent to care and treatment

evidenceCategory.commentary:
The service told patients about their rights around consent and respected these when delivering person-centred care and treatment.

Staff followed the provider’s policies on consent to treatment. Across both wards, 100% of staff had completed training in the Mental Capacity Act 2005 and Deprivation of Liberty Safeguards.

Staff took all practical steps to enable patients to make their own decisions. For patients who might have impaired mental capacity, staff assessed and recorded capacity to consent appropriately, on a decision-specific basis. In the care and treatment records we viewed, capacity discussions relating to medication, finances and treatment decisions were clearly documented.

Staff recorded patients’ consent to involve carers in their care, or whether they chose to decline this. With consent in place, staff supported carers to be involved in patients’ care and discharge planning.

topicareas.qualityStatementscore: 3 - Evidence shows a good standard of care

topicareas.name: Delivering evidence-based care and treatment

evidenceCategory.commentary:
The service planned and delivered patients’ care and treatment with them, including what was important and mattered to them. They did this in line with legislation and current evidence-based good practice and standards.

Staff delivered a range of care and treatment interventions which were recommended by guidance from the National Institute for Health and Care Excellence (NICE). These included medication and psychological therapies. On both New Dawn and Upping wards, staff provided DBT (dialectical behavioural therapy), compassion focused therapy (CFT), CBT (cognitive behavioural therapy) and eye movement desensitisation reprocessing (EMDR). New Dawn offered a more structured DBT programme. The care and treatment records demonstrated that care was provided in line with current guidance, with well-embedded psychology input. We reviewed psychology formulation records for 2 patients. Both records demonstrated high quality and were holistic and personalised.

Due to patients’ complex presentations often associated with trauma, care was trauma informed. On both wards, 100% of staff had completed mandatory training in trauma informed care.

Care records showed that patients engaged in a broad programme of therapeutic activities in one-to-one and group settings. These included psychology sessions, self-care support groups, workshops, games, cinema, recovery college, social club, arts and crafts, pampering, and exercise. Patients we spoke with were positive about the choice and availability of activities on offer.

The multidisciplinary team (MDT) included, or had access to, the full range of specialists required to meet the needs of patients. These were doctors and nurses, psychologists, psychotherapists, occupational therapists (OTs), social therapists, dietitians, social workers, activity practitioners, and experts by experience.

Staff participated in clinical audit and quality improvement (QI) initiatives. The audit schedule covered physical health, care planning, medicines, restrictive practices, primary nurse sessions, and family and carer contacts. Psychology team carried out audits to evaluate ward atmosphere. Physical healthcare was an area of current quality improvement focus, and staff told us about an ongoing project on weight management.

Staff had access to regular team meetings, reflective practice, debriefs, peer support, professional supervision, and specialist training and development. Support staff received training in DBT and personality disorders. OT staff were trained in sensory integration and supported wider team development in this, including presenting at a recent awayday.

topicareas.qualityStatementscore: 3 - Evidence shows a good standard of care

topicareas.name: How staff, teams and services work together

evidenceCategory.commentary:
The service worked well across teams and services to support patients. They shared their assessment of patients’ needs when they moved between different services.

Staff shared key information about patients in daily huddles and handover meetings. Staff described handovers as comprehensive, and permanent staff additionally briefed bank and agency colleagues on patient-specific risks. Staff we spoke with described working well together as a multidisciplinary team (MDT). Disciplines including nursing, psychology, social work and allied health professions were well-embedded. The care and treatment records we viewed reflected MDT discussions and decision-making.

The MDT meetings we observed were well-attended by the professionals. However, some staff said that managerial and clinical governance meetings often overran.

The service worked well with other teams within the provider group and externally. Key system partners included NHS commissioners, local authorities, GPs, secondary care, and community mental health teams. GPs and dentists attended the wards regularly, and women’s health screening was carried out by the local hospital. Staff involved care coordinators by inviting them to ward rounds, although we heard they did not always attend. A care coordinator joined 1 of the 2 ward rounds we observed. Staff offered Care and Treatment Reviews (CTRs) to autistic patients in line with statutory requirements. CTR is a person-centred review with an independent panel to ensure that care is delivered in the least restrictive way. However, for one patient recently diagnosed with autism a CTR had not yet been completed.

topicareas.qualityStatementscore: 3 - Evidence shows a good standard of care

topicareas.name: Monitoring and improving outcomes

evidenceCategory.commentary:
The service routinely monitored patients’ care and treatment to continuously improve it. They ensured that outcomes were positive and consistent, and that they met both clinical expectations and the expectations of patients themselves.

In the care and treatment records we viewed and ward rounds we observed, we saw evidence that staff used recognised scales and outcome measures. These included Glasgow Antipsychotic Side-effect Scale (GASS), Dialog+ (questionnaire to assess patient satisfaction and needs), and the National Early Warning Score (NEWS2). In one ward round, staff reviewed and discussed the GASS score with the patient, alongside the medication and its side effects.

We identified an area for improvement in relation to NEWS2 record keeping, particularly following incidents of self-harm. We discussed with staff that this could be strengthened by clearly documenting rationale when discontinuing monitoring, or when scores are escalated. We were assured that the recently appointed physical health lead had already identified this through audits and had taken steps to reinforce the correct processes to staff.

Staff we spoke with confirmed they had the time and opportunities to participate in clinical audits and quality improvement activities.

topicareas.qualityStatementscore: 3 - Evidence shows a good standard of care

topicareas.name: Supporting people to live healthier lives

evidenceCategory.commentary:
The service supported patients to manage their health and wellbeing to maximise their independence, choice and control. The service supported patients to live healthier lives and where possible, reduce their future needs for care and support.

There were activities on offer to help promote a healthy lifestyle for patients. These included facilitated gym sessions, mindfulness, nature walks, smoothie making, one-to-one cooking sessions, and weekly smoking cessation groups. All clinical staff received training in smoking cessation, and the service supplied nicotine replacement products to patients. Therapy animals visited the hospital to promote mental wellbeing. There was an incentive scheme linked to patient participation in gym sessions, with prizes available. Sessions offered through Sports for Confidence (an initiative to widen access to physical activity) such as swimming, aqua aerobics and racquet sports took place twice a week at a local sports centre.

Staff referred patients to a dietitian, who liaised with the physical health lead and kitchen staff about individual needs.

Posters promoting women’s health screenings were displayed prominently on the wards. Further work was planned to strengthen staff and patient education around women’s health.

topicareas.qualityStatementscore: 3 - Evidence shows a good standard of care

keyQuestionRatings.name: Responsive
keyQuestionRatings.commentary:
This means we looked for evidence that the service met people’s needs.

At our last assessment we rated this key question good. At this assessment the rating has remained good.

This meant people’s needs were met through good organisation and delivery.

topicareas.name: Care provision, Integration and continuity

evidenceCategory.commentary:
The service understood the diverse health and care needs of patients and their local communities, so care was joined-up, flexible and supported choice and continuity.

Staff ensured that patients could access work, training and education opportunities while at hospital. For example, a patient we spoke with told us about completing an access course during their admission, and was preparing to start a degree course following discharge. They were very positive about the support they had received from staff.

The service had developed dedicated carer provision. Each ward had a nominated carer champion, and there was a well-established friends and family newsletter. The newsletter shared information on available support resources and news about the service. Regular carer forums were held face-to-face and online. Staff also told us about good links with external partners, such as local carer support groups and education services.

Staff supported and encouraged patients to maintain contact with their families and friends, in line with their wishes. Some patients told us about going on home leave. Patients who did not have leave received visits at the hospital and could keep in touch using their own phones.

Staff involved other relevant services as appropriate, including the local acute hospital, GPs, community teams and NHS commissioners. When patients were admitted out of area, their carers and other professionals involved in their care could join the ward rounds virtually.

Stakeholders we spoke with said the service was good at providing care and forward planning.

topicareas.qualityStatementscore: 3 - Evidence shows a good standard of care

topicareas.name: Equity in access

evidenceCategory.commentary:
The service made sure that people could access the care, support and treatment they needed when they needed it.

Each ward had inclusion and exclusion criteria to ensure it could meet patients’ needs safely. Local clinical teams reviewed incoming referrals and made decisions about the most appropriate pathway. We saw evidence that the service had declined some inappropriate referrals.

The hospital was accessible for people with mobility needs. The building was equipped with lifts and evacuation chairs. Personal Emergency Evacuation Plans (PEEPs) were completed for patients where required. PEEPs were detailed, individualised and reflected patient-specific needs.

Staff ensured that patients had access to appropriate care pre- and post-discharge and planned for this jointly with them, carers and relevant professionals.

topicareas.qualityStatementscore: 3 - Evidence shows a good standard of care

topicareas.name: Equity in experiences and outcomes

evidenceCategory.commentary:
Staff and leaders actively listened to information about patients who are most likely to experience inequality in experience or outcomes and tailored their care, support and treatment in response to this.

Staff we spoke with thought the service was inclusive of diverse groups of people, including those with protected characteristics under the Equality Act 2010. All staff on both wards had completed mandatory training in equity and diversity and the Oliver McGowan mandatory training on learning disability and autism. There was information displayed on the wards to make people welcome and included, for example carers and LGBTQ+ communities.

Staff told us about making personalised adjustments for people with protected characteristics. Staff demonstrated a good awareness of women-specific health issues and the related health inequalities. The hospital’s physical health lead planned further education for staff and patients around women’s health by introducing monthly sessions on each ward.

The service offered comprehensive carer support. A carer we spoke with confirmed they had been invited to carers’ groups.

topicareas.qualityStatementscore: 3 - Evidence shows a good standard of care

topicareas.name: Listening to and involving people

evidenceCategory.commentary:
The service made it easy for patients to share feedback and ideas, or raise complaints about their care, treatment and support. They involved patients in decisions about their care and told them what had changed as a result.

Staff ensured that patients had opportunities to be involved in shaping the service. Patients could raise their queries or concerns at weekly community meetings. We attended 2 community meetings which were chaired by patients. They were conducted collaboratively and well-attended by patients and staff. Patients we spoke with confirmed they attended community meetings regularly and received feedback. ‘You said, we did’ boards were updated following community meetings.

There were monthly people’s council meetings attended by patient representatives and staff. Patients told us about delivering training on personality disorders to staff, and were part of staff recruitment panels. Patients were involved in choosing furniture and colours for the wards and the family room. Patient artwork was on display throughout the hospital.

The provider’s expert by experience visited the hospital regularly. They were committed to strengthening co-production, trauma informed care and patient empowerment. They felt their role was valued by the service, which helped to improve two-way feedback between staff and patients.

The service conducted regular patient and carer surveys. The most recent surveys were completed from March to June 2026. The themes in responses generally echoed the feedback we heard from patients, staff and carers. For example, some respondents wanted better food and more regular updates.

Patients told us they knew how to complain if needed, apart from one who said they did not but would ask for a complaints form. A carer we spoke with said they could give feedback to the service through a survey, and would call the ward in the first instance if they needed to complain.

Information on how to complain was available throughout the hospital. People could complain in several ways, including through email, QR code or in writing. Staff handled complaints appropriately and managers were trained in complaint investigation. Senior managers oversaw complaints and feedback and monitored themes and trends. In the 6 months leading up to our inspection, the hospital received 33 complaints and 50 compliments. Most complaints related to quality of care, lost or damaged property and staff attitude. Lessons learnt were shared in clinical governance and business meetings. Feedback from complaints was shared in staff meetings or one-to-one if related to an individual. We heard about changes made in response to complaints, such as improving one-to-one sessions, reviewing cultural and spiritual support information, and taking steps to improve the food menu.

topicareas.qualityStatementscore: 3 - Evidence shows a good standard of care

topicareas.name: Person-centred Care

evidenceCategory.commentary:
The service made sure patients were at the centre of their care and treatment choices and they decided, in partnership with patients, how to respond to any relevant changes in their needs.

The care and treatment records we reviewed demonstrated that care planning was personalised and patients had a voice in their care. Staff we spoke with told us about their strong commitment to supporting patients with complex presentations through personalised, culturally-sensitive care. Patients told us that staff supported them to understand and manage their own risks better. Two patients shared examples of how this approach had helped them to reduce behaviours that previously led to harm or incidents.

There were activities on offer to suit different interests, available one-to-one and in groups. Patients were positive about the choice of activities. In addition to ward-based activities, there were organised walks and sports sessions in the community. Faith leaders visited the wards to meet with patients.

Staff empowered patients to make their own decisions about their care and treatment. Patients provided feedback at their ward rounds and staff discussed it with them.

topicareas.qualityStatementscore: 3 - Evidence shows a good standard of care

topicareas.name: Planning for the future

evidenceCategory.commentary:
Patients were supported to plan for important life changes, so they could have enough time to make informed decisions about their future.

Staff involved patients and where applicable, their carers, in making decisions about their care. Care planning reflected patients’ and carers’ views. Discussions about treatment goals started at pre-admission stage.

Staff ensured that all relevant teams and professionals were involved in planning the care and treatment of patients with complex needs, including when patients were admitted from out of area. These included local authorities, GPs, community teams and NHS commissioners. Care coordinators were invited to ward rounds.

There was a small number of patients on Upping Ward whose needs had evolved since referral and exceeded those the service could meet safely. Staff were working to identify more appropriate placements for these patients. Shortly after our site visit, we heard that one of these patients had been successfully transferred to a more suitable placement.

Due to the level of complexity often involved, lengths of stay at hospital varied. Sometimes discharges were delayed for patients who were clinically ready due to circumstances outside of the service’s control, such as supported accommodation or social care availability. Managers monitored discharge forecasts for each patient. A patient we spoke with on New Dawn Ward told us about their discharge plans. However, one carer of a patient on Upping Ward said they were not aware of the discharge plan. One partner agency stakeholder thought that discharge planning could be further strengthened through clearer goal setting and implementing positive risk-taking management planning.

topicareas.qualityStatementscore: 3 - Evidence shows a good standard of care

topicareas.name: Providing Information

evidenceCategory.commentary:
The service supplied appropriate, accurate and up-to-date information in formats that were tailored to individual needs.

Staff communicated with patients in line with their individual communication needs and preferences documented in the care plan. For example, staff tailored communication for neurodivergent patients.

Staff ensured that patients could access essential information, such as treatments, their rights, key contacts, independent advocacy, interpreter service and how to complain. Community meeting outcomes were displayed on ‘you said, we did’ boards. Actions taken in response to patient feedback included environmental improvements and maintenance requests. Tailored information was available for patients and carers.

Carers were mostly positive about communication with and from the service and the information they received. However, one carer said they were not updated regularly and staff did not call them back when requested. The results of the most recent carer survey indicated that some respondents wanted more regular updates.

Staff regularly updated commissioners and other professionals involved in patients’ care. The service submitted appropriate notifications to the relevant external bodies. A partner agency stakeholder described staff as prompt in responding to queries.

topicareas.qualityStatementscore: 3 - Evidence shows a good standard of care

keyQuestionRatings.name: Safe
keyQuestionRatings.commentary:
This means we looked for evidence that people were protected from abuse and avoidable harm.

At our last assessment we rated this key question requires improvement. The service was previously in breach of regulations in relation to safe care and treatment and staffing. At this assessment the rating has improved to good. We found significant improvements in the previous areas of concern, and the service was no longer in breach of regulations.

This meant people were safe and protected from avoidable harm.

topicareas.name: Infection prevention and control

evidenceCategory.commentary:
The service assessed and managed the risk of infection. They detected and controlled the risk of it spreading and shared concerns with appropriate agencies promptly.

The ward environment was visibly clean, with appropriate well-maintained furnishings. Staff maintained clinical equipment well and kept it clean.

Staff adhered to infection control principles, with 100% of staff across both wards up-to-date with the mandatory infection control (IPC) and food safety training. The hospital’s physical health lead was also the IPC lead, and there were IPC leads on each ward.

Cleaning records were completed daily and demonstrated that all ward areas were cleaned regularly. Communal areas were cleaned throughout the week, and routine bedroom cleaning was undertaken during weekdays. Patients we spoke with did not report concerns about cleanliness.

topicareas.qualityStatementscore: 3 - Evidence shows a good standard of care

topicareas.name: Involving people to manage risks

evidenceCategory.commentary:
The service worked with people to understand and manage risks by thinking holistically. Staff assessed and managed risks to patients and themselves well and followed best practice in anticipating, de-escalating and managing challenging behaviour. Staff used restraint only after attempts at de-escalation had failed. Staff participated in the provider’s restrictive interventions reduction programme. They provided care to meet patients’ needs that was safe, supportive and enabled them to do the things that mattered to them.

Staff we spoke with demonstrated a good understanding of patients and their individual risks. The risks, and any changes to those, were discussed in daily huddles and handovers. We spoke with 5 patients, who told us they felt safe at the hospital. Patients said that staff supported them to understand their own risks better. However, 2 patients said they felt less safe during incidents involving other patients.

We viewed 8 care and treatment records. Records included a safety summary, providing a clear, at-a-glance crisis management plan. Individual crisis management plans were displayed in each patient’s bedroom. Care plans were holistic, with clear evidence of patient and carer involvement, and were reviewed monthly during ward rounds with patient input. Risk assessments were up to date and reflected recent multidisciplinary team (MDT) discussions and current risks. The hospital recently adopted a safety formulation approach, reflecting current best practice guidance. This meant the wards had moved from older risk assessment models. For example, for one patient there was a discussion about how best to support them during self-harm episodes, including consideration of alternatives to restraint.

Staff demonstrated commitment to reducing restrictive practices and using restraint only as the last resort. Managers monitored and reviewed every incident requiring restraint. In the current year leading up to our inspection, New Dawn Ward reported 33 incidents of rapid tranquilisation (RT) and Upping Ward 36. There were 8 instances of prone restraint on Upping Ward during the same time, and 7 on New Dawn. These related to a small number of patients, one of whom had since been transferred to a more appropriate placement. Incident records detailed the reason for restraint, including whether it was patient or staff-led. Each restraint followed unsuccessful de-escalation attempts in response to significant risks and was typically of very short duration. Managers met with staff individually after each instance. There was no use of seclusion or long-term segregation during the same period.

Two dedicated Prevention and Management of Violence and Aggression (PMVA) leads supported staff and patients. PMVA leads and managers completed joint reviews of restraints using CCTV. Staff compliance with PMVA and relational security training was over 97% on both wards, and all new starters were trained in PMVA prior to starting work. Safety pods were available on each ward.

Most patients who had been restrained told us they understood the reason for this, and said that staff had done so safely and considerately. Patients received debriefs following incidents of restraint. However, one patient was less happy with how their restraint had been carried out, and said they had not received a debrief.

Staff carried out different levels of observations and reviewed these based on individual need and risk. All eligible staff had completed training in observation and engagement. We viewed a sample of observation records, which had been completed consistently, with details of patients’ presentation at each observation point. Patients we spoke with knew what level of observations they were on, and the rationale for this. One patient told us how staff had worked jointly with them to reduce their observation levels. The occupational therapy (OT) team had introduced an engagement resource box containing low-risk games, hot chocolate, and sensory items to help nursing staff build rapport with patients on close observations.

topicareas.qualityStatementscore: 3 - Evidence shows a good standard of care

topicareas.name: Learning culture

evidenceCategory.commentary:
The service had a proactive and positive culture of safety, based on openness and honesty. They listened to concerns about safety and investigated and reported safety events. Lessons were learnt to continually identify and embed good practice.

Staff knew what incidents to report and how to report them, with 100% compliance in incident reporting training across both wards. In the current year leading up to our inspection, New Dawn Ward reported 625 incidents and Upping Ward 651. The leading cause of incidents related to deliberate self-harm. All physical restraints and administration of rapid tranquilisation (RT), including ‘when required’ (PRN) medicines, were reported as incidents.

Managers monitored themes and trends closely and implemented actions to prevent reoccurrence. The safeguarding team provided feedback on safeguarding incidents. Managers carried out after action reviews (AAR) following serious incidents. Staff we spoke with shared examples of learning from recent incidents, and what changed as a result. For example, managers were planning sensory improvements on Upping Ward because they had identified that noise contributed to an increase in incidents. On New Dawn, we heard about learning implemented around crisis planning and relational security.

We reviewed a sample of incident records across the wards which demonstrated an appropriate level of detail and actions taken. Managers reviewed all incidents in line with the provider’s policy. Feedback was provided to staff through the incident reporting form.

Support was available to patients and staff following incidents, including debriefs with psychology staff and coaching support. For example, a patient we spoke with on New Dawn Ward told us they were offered debriefs with familiar staff, who discussed what had happened and how to prevent it from happening again.

Staff reported a positive learning culture within the service. Staff and managers discussed incidents and learning arising in daily huddles, supervision, and weekly and monthly meetings. Learning from the wider hospital and the provider group was shared in newsletters, meetings and induction. Folders with learning bulletins were also available for staff to read in the nursing offices.

topicareas.qualityStatementscore: 3 - Evidence shows a good standard of care

topicareas.name: Medicines optimisation

evidenceCategory.commentary:
The service made sure that medicines and treatments were safe and met patients’ needs, capacities and preferences. They involved patients in planning, including when changes happened.

The service had improved its medicines management since our last inspection, and patients now received their medicines safely as prescribed. Staff told us the external pharmacy provider now worked more reliably. There were also contingency plans in place to obtain medicines from a local pharmacy if needed. A new electronic prescribing and medicines administration (ePMA) system had just been launched within the hospital, reducing reliance on paper records.

Staff regularly reviewed the effects of medicines on each person's mental and physical health. Staff told us the pharmacist visited the unit weekly, and we saw evidence that pharmacists checked the legality of prescriptions and informed prescribers if there were any issues. We saw evidence that Mental Health Act consent to treatment forms were in place and verified by the pharmacist.

Rapid tranquilisation (RT), the process of administering a medicine intramuscularly for rapid sedation, was used as a last resort. Staff actively worked to use alternative person-centred ways to de-escalate without the need to administer RT. We saw evidence that when patients were given RT, they were appropriately monitored. When PRN (‘when required’) medicines were used the reason for their use and what else had been tried first was clearly recorded on the daily electronic care records.

Staff monitored the side effects patients experienced from their medicines using the Glasgow antipsychotic side effect scale (GASS) monitoring scales and made adjustments where needed.

Patients we spoke with confirmed they had enough information about their medicines. One patient said they had been informed about the side effects, and another told us how changes to their medicines were discussed and agreed with them in every ward round.

Medicines were stored safely and securely within the locked treatment room. Staff had access to controlled drugs storage facilities that met legal requirements.
