Temperature readings for medicines storage areas were appropriately monitored and within recommended range. Emergency medicines and equipment were in place and checked regularly. The external pharmacy service provided a TTA (to take away) supply service, and dispensing for unplanned discharges or overnight leave could be undertaken in-house by nursing staff. We saw a sample of TTA medicines labels and instructions staff used when preparing discharge medicines, and these did not include cautionary labels.

The provider had a system in place to ensure staff knew about safety alerts. Staff told us that medicines-related incidents were reported and investigated. The pharmacist produced a medicines report on themes, trends and incidents for the monthly governance committee meeting.

topicareas.qualityStatementscore: 3 - Evidence shows a good standard of care

topicareas.name: Safe and effective staffing

evidenceCategory.commentary:
The service made sure there were enough qualified, skilled and experienced staff, who received effective support, supervision and development. They worked together well to provide safe care that met patients’ individual needs.

The service was fully staffed to safely meet the needs of patients. We saw staff always present in communal areas and engaging with patients. Patients we spoke with told us they had weekly one-to-one sessions with their primary nurse. Most did not report concerns about staff availability for escorted leave.

There was a small number of vacancies on each ward, in various stages of recruitment and onboarding. These were covered with cross-cover arrangements or locum staff.

Managers had calculated the safe staffing levels for each ward, which were reviewed daily and adjusted according to the changing needs. The service could deploy their own bank and agency staff who were familiar with the wards, or request staff from other Cygnet hospitals.

In the recent months, Upping Ward experienced an increase in safety incidents related to a small number of patients, requiring them to be nursed on enhanced and continuous observations. This had resulted in staffing pressures, which managers identified and mitigated by increasing the staffing levels. Staff we spoke with did not report concerns about present staffing levels. However, some staff reflected on the challenges in supporting patients with high levels of distress, the emotional impact of this and the resulting workload pressures. Although patients did not generally report concerns about staffing, 2 patients on Upping Ward thought that more staff would be beneficial due to the intensive support required for some peers and resulting incidents.

There was adequate medical cover day and night and a doctor could attend quickly in an emergency. Staff received training in responding to emergencies and basic and immediate life support, and staff on both wards were compliant with this training. Unannounced emergency simulation drills took place weekly.

Staff participated in regular training, appraisal and supervision, and managers monitored the completion rates. These were now consistently high. On New Dawn Ward, 89% of staff were compliant with mandatory training and 92% with clinical supervision. On Upping Ward, 98% were up-to-date with mandatory training and 92% with clinical supervision. Compliance with appraisal was 90% across both wards. All staff on both wards had now completed the Oliver McGowan mandatory training on learning disability and autism.

The service had now implemented a robust process to monitor bank staff compliance with training and supervision. Mandatory training compliance was at 95% and clinical supervision 93% for bank support workers. Mandatory training for bank nurses was at 90%, however clinical supervision compliance was lower at 52% at the time of our inspection. Managers ensured that shift allocation was put on hold for staff until compliance had been achieved. Shortly after our site visit, managers provided evidence of bank nursing staff supervision being completed, achieving 90% compliance.

The service followed procedures for safe recruitment of staff. This included criminal record and right to work checks, and where relevant, evidence of continued professional registration. Managers had now implemented additional audits to monitor continuous compliance with employment checks.

topicareas.qualityStatementscore: 3 - Evidence shows a good standard of care

topicareas.name: Safe environments

evidenceCategory.commentary:
Staff detected and controlled potential risks in the care environment. They made sure equipment, facilities and technology supported the delivery of safe care.

Staff assessed and managed environmental risks well. There were daily and weekly security checks and safety huddles. Staff had access to alarms, and bedrooms had nurse call systems. Staff completed risk assessments for potential ligature anchor points and mitigated the risks adequately. Staff completed relevant mandatory training, with 100% compliance in ligature risk reduction, fire warden and health & safety training.

Fire safety arrangements were robust, with regular testing and evidence of learning from evacuation drills. Detailed personal emergency evacuation plans (PEEPs) were in place for patients. The hospital fire alarm system was due to be upgraded in June 2026.

Staff followed procedures to keep patients safe from harm by completing room and personal searches as needed. There were 2 storage areas to manage personal effects and restricted items safely. A security nurse was allocated daily to carry out health and safety checks, and each ward had security champions. CCTV was in operation in communal areas and its records were used to review incidents.

The service environment was well-maintained and recovery focused. Patients had access to enclosed outdoor areas, activity room, indoor gym, and a social hub. The social hub was a welcoming area away from the ward environment. It was equipped with massage chairs, interactive games, a nail bar, and sensory resources. The kitchen and laundry room were accessible with staff supervision, in line with individual risk assessments. However, the activities of daily living (ADL) kitchen lacked sufficient ventilation. Staff continued accessing the social hub while it was used by patients, which resulted in interruptions and potential impact on its therapeutic value.

Staff recognised that the hospital environment could be improved to support the needs of neurodivergent patients better. The service had developed sensory heat maps. There was work planned to make the wards more autism-friendly, for example dimmable lights and sound absorbing sheets. The hospital-wide alarm system was noisy. It was due to be replaced in July 2026, and staff expected this to improve.

The service had access to a seclusion room within the hospital, although the use of seclusion was rare.

Patients had had personalised their bedrooms which they could access throughout the day. Patients were not provided with their own bedroom keys, as identical locks were used throughout the hospital. Each bedroom had an ensuite toilet and sink, and there were shared shower and bath facilities on each ward. Patients could raise maintenance issues in weekly community meetings.

Clinic rooms had appropriate equipment that was checked and calibrated regularly. Emergency equipment including ligature cutters and clinic room grab bags were stored appropriately and were easily accessible. However, on Upping Ward the procedure for checking ligature cutting equipment needed updating to record the contents more accurately.

topicareas.qualityStatementscore: 3 - Evidence shows a good standard of care

topicareas.name: Safe systems, pathways and transitions

evidenceCategory.commentary:
The service worked with patients and healthcare partners to establish and maintain safe systems of care, in which safety was managed or monitored. They made sure there was continuity of care, including when patients moved between different services.

The service received referrals from NHS commissioners through the provider’s referral hub. The referral and admission processes aimed to ensure that all essential information about the patient was received to determine if their needs could be met safely. Staff discussed upcoming admissions and discharges in daily huddles, handovers and monthly meetings.

Local clinical teams reviewed referral information and made decisions about the most appropriate pathway and ward. Both wards followed their inclusion and exclusion criteria, and the service had declined some referrals for patients whose needs it could not meet safely. New Dawn Ward was separated into 2 areas, New Dawn 1 (12 beds) and New Dawn 2 (6 beds). Patients were allocated to each area in line with their needs, with New Dawn 2 providing more intensive support during crises or increased distress.

At our last inspection, most patients were admitted out of area, which meant they were away from their home areas, families and friends. At this inspection, more admissions were now local, from London and the home counties. The service recently declined some referrals that were very far out of area. The service could also redirect referrals to other Cygnet hospitals closer to the patient’s local area.

Staff involved relevant health and social care services to ensure patients had continuity of safe care, both within the service and post-discharge. These included commissioners, acute hospitals, GP and community teams. There was an informal buddy system for new patients on admission, promoting peer support. Staff supported patients to prepare for discharge safely, for example with Care Programme Approach (CPA) support, overnight leave to future placements, and activities of daily living (ADL) assessments.

At the time of our inspection, the needs of a small number of patients admitted to Upping Ward exceeded those the service was able to meet safely. Managers explained that the presentations of these patients had evolved significantly since initial assessment. This had an impact on safety, resulting in increased incidents. Staff were proactively working with the patients’ home teams to identify more appropriate placements for them. We heard that one of these patients had been successfully transferred to a more suitable placement shortly after our site visit.

Staff planned for patients’ safe discharge. In a ward round we attended, staff discussed and agreed plans with a patient who was due to be discharged shortly, including crisis planning and family involvement.

topicareas.qualityStatementscore: 3 - Evidence shows a good standard of care

topicareas.name: Safeguarding

evidenceCategory.commentary:
The service worked with patients and healthcare partners to understand what being safe meant to them and the best way to achieve that. They concentrated on improving patients’ lives while protecting their right to live in safety, free from bullying, harassment, abuse, discrimination, avoidable harm and neglect. The service shared safeguarding concerns quickly and appropriately.

The service had robust safeguarding systems in place. Over 93% of staff on both wards were trained in safeguarding to the level in line with their role. Safeguarding was discussed as part of supervision and team meetings, and staff received quarterly safeguarding supervision. Learning was shared internally through email newsletters, meetings and individual supervision, and shared externally with the local authority team.

Patients and carers we spoke with reported that they, or their relatives, felt safe on the wards. However, 2 patients and 1 carer said they (or their relative) sometimes felt less safe during incidents involving other patients.

The service had a safeguarding lead who was embedded in the multidisciplinary team and easily accessible to staff. The lead supported managers in reviewing incidents and attended weekly meetings involving all managers. Staff we spoke with were positive about the input of the social work team, describing it as very responsive. For example, we heard how the social work team had helped develop a coordinated approach for a patient with complex needs in response to an increase in incidents.

We heard that the service had built good working relationships and effective mechanisms to link with the local authority. In the care and treatment records we viewed, safeguarding referrals had been completed where relevant.

Due to increasingly complex needs of patients, there was a dedicated social worker on each ward. At the time of our inspection, Upping Ward had a vacancy for a social worker which had been recruited to.

The hospital admitted female patients only. Patients could request to work with a female primary nurse, if preferred. Referrals for transgender patients were subject to an individual risk assessment in line with the provider’s policy.

There was a protocol in place for visitors to the hospital. The multidisciplinary team (MDT) screened visits, and the social work team risk assessed children’s visits. Visits with children took place in the dedicated visitors’ room.

The provider’s central team led on and oversaw safeguarding audits. Further training was planned to upskill staff on making safeguarding referrals. The service was in the process of developing its electronic safeguarding dashboard to enable integration with the incident reporting system.

The hospital maintained a blanket restriction register and reviewed it quarterly. There were some restrictions in place which were proportionate to maintain a healthy and safe environment. For example, staff risk assessed and supervised patient access to the kitchen. Patients did not raise concerns about blanket restrictions. Patients were involved in these discussions through community meetings, and we heard that patients recently raised 2 restrictions which were due to be reviewed.

topicareas.qualityStatementscore: 3 - Evidence shows a good standard of care

keyQuestionRatings.name: Well-led
keyQuestionRatings.commentary:
This means we looked for evidence that service leadership, management and governance assured high-quality, person-centred care; supported learning and innovation; and promoted an open, fair culture.

At our last assessment we rated this key question requires improvement. At this assessment the rating has improved to good. The service had made tangible improvements in its governance systems and was no longer in breach of regulations.

This meant the service was consistently managed and well-led. Leaders and the culture they created promoted high-quality, person-centred care.

topicareas.name: Capable, compassionate and inclusive leaders

evidenceCategory.commentary:
The service had inclusive leaders at all levels who understood the context in which they delivered care, treatment and support and embodied the culture and values of their workforce and organisation. Leaders had the skills, knowledge, experience and credibility to lead effectively. They did so with integrity, openness and honesty.

Since our last inspection, the service had appointed new leaders. The new managers had the skills, knowledge and competence to perform their roles, and a good understanding of the service they managed. Leaders demonstrated commitment to improving the areas of concern identified in our previous inspection and were aware where there was still more work to do. We saw tangible improvements in the governance systems at this inspection.

Staff we spoke with reported confidence in the local leadership. They described the managers as visible, approachable, supportive and responsive.

Training and development opportunities were available for staff. For example, we heard about some support workers training to become nurses. Several managers we met had progressed to their current roles after working for the provider since qualifying.

topicareas.qualityStatementscore: 3 - Evidence shows a good standard of care

topicareas.name: Freedom to speak up

evidenceCategory.commentary:
The service fostered a positive culture where people felt they could speak up and their voice would be heard.

Staff we spoke with described a positive and open culture and said they were comfortable to raise concerns with managers if needed. Freedom to Speak Up (FTSU) information was clearly displayed, and each ward had a FTSU champion. Staff knew about the FTSU and whistleblowing arrangements.

Patients could raise concerns at weekly community meetings. ‘You said, we did’ feedback was displayed on the ward information boards. Patient representatives were involved in decision-making about the service. The service regularly collected feedback from carers through surveys.

Managers monitored feedback and complaints received. Staff discussed learning and themes identified from these.

topicareas.qualityStatementscore: 3 - Evidence shows a good standard of care

topicareas.name: Governance, management and sustainability

evidenceCategory.commentary:
The service had clear responsibilities, roles, systems of accountability and good governance. They used these to manage and deliver good quality, sustainable care, treatment and support. They acted on the best information about risk, performance and outcomes, and shared this securely with others when appropriate.

The service now had robust governance systems in place that supported safe and effective care delivery. There was now improved assurance that physical health monitoring and medicines administration were carried out in line with the provider’s expectations and national guidance. Leaders monitored audit outcomes so they were acted on. Staff said that oversight had improved and leaders proactively followed up any actions. Leaders now closely monitored staff compliance with training, supervision and employment checks. They had put effective mechanisms in place and took timely action when any non-compliance was identified.

There was a clear framework of what must be discussed in meetings at a ward, hospital and provider level to ensure that essential information was shared. Staff had implemented recommendations from reviews of incidents and complaints. We saw evidence of changes made as a result of learning.

The risk register detailed an appropriate range of risks specific to the hospital and was regularly reviewed. A business continuity plan was in place to ensure service delivery could continue in the event of emergency, such as adverse weather or staffing shortages.

Information systems had improved since our last inspection. The electronic patient record system now enabled more efficient record keeping and integration with audits. The hospital had just launched a new electronic prescribing and medicines administration (ePMA) system, reducing reliance on paper records. The service was developing its electronic safeguarding dashboard to streamline reporting through integration with the incident reporting system. Over 97% of staff across both wards had completed training in information governance.

topicareas.qualityStatementscore: 3 - Evidence shows a good standard of care

topicareas.name: Learning, improvement and innovation

evidenceCategory.commentary:
The service focused on continuous learning, innovation and improvement across the organisation and local system. They encouraged creative ways of delivering equality of experience, outcome and quality of life for patients. They actively contributed to safe, effective practice and research.

Innovation and quality improvement (QI) activities were taking place within the service. Staff held weekly practice QI meetings where they discussed ideas for improving practice. Recent and ongoing QI projects included staff retention, weight management for patients, and recycling initiatives on the wards.

Staff told us about innovative practice. For example, staff on Upping Ward told us about introducing safety cutlery which would not cause harm if ingested by a patient. Staff also recently introduced credit-card sized crisis plan cards for every patient on the ward which they carried on their lanyards. We heard how this enabled staff to respond quicker and offer personalised support without having to consult electronic or paper records.

The service was accredited through the Enabling Environments framework, a Royal College of Psychiatrists’ initiative focused on improving the quality of relationships and culture within services. The whole hospital had achieved accreditation with Triangle of Care, a quality improvement scheme aimed at improving support for carers.

topicareas.qualityStatementscore: 3 - Evidence shows a good standard of care

topicareas.name: Partnerships and communities

evidenceCategory.commentary:
The service understood their duty to collaborate and work in partnership, so services work seamlessly for patients. They shared information and learning with partners and collaborated for improvement.

The service worked with external stakeholders including primary and secondary care, community teams, commissioners and local authorities. Staff involved key system partners when providing complex care.

Staff had developed links with other organisations in supporting people who faced additional barriers or inequalities. These included local carer support groups and Sports for Confidence, a community-based service aimed at improving access to physical activity for underserved groups. Staff worked with a local hospital to provide women’s health and sexual health screenings.

We received feedback from stakeholders who regularly worked with the service. They described a positive experience of working with the service as a partner agency.

topicareas.qualityStatementscore: 3 - Evidence shows a good standard of care

topicareas.name: Shared direction and culture

evidenceCategory.commentary:
The service had a shared vision, strategy and culture. This was based on transparency, equity, equality and human rights, diversity and inclusion, engagement, and understanding challenges and the needs of people and their communities.

The provider’s values were visible throughout the hospital and were part of mandatory training, which staff on both wards had completed. Staff supervision and appraisal records were linked to the values. Staff said they were proud to work for the provider and told us about applying its values in their work. They were confident that equity, diversity and inclusion were embedded in day-to-day practice through coproduction, culturally sensitive care, and recognition of patients' individual needs and preferences.

Patients had a voice in decision-making. Patients were involved in community and people’s council meetings, and participated in staff recruitment and training. Patients could access training, volunteering and employment.

Staff had opportunities to contribute to discussions about the service. In addition to staff meetings, the service organised awaydays where staff discussed teamwork, culture and future service improvements.

Staff could provide feedback through annual surveys. Most recent surveys on both wards were conducted in 2026, and their results were generally consistent with the feedback we heard from staff. For example, some respondents reported dissatisfaction with their workload and staffing levels. Most respondents were positive about their team and the provider, managerial support, and both their own and the service’s commitment to quality patient care.

topicareas.qualityStatementscore: 3 - Evidence shows a good standard of care

topicareas.name: Workforce equality, diversity and inclusion

evidenceCategory.commentary:
The service valued diversity in their workforce. They worked towards an inclusive and fair culture by improving equality and equity for people who work for them.

All staff had completed training in equity, diversity and promoting human rights. Staff we spoke with were confident that the service was open and inclusive for diverse groups of people, with equal opportunities for training and development available. For example, some staff shared how colleagues were supportive of their religious needs. Staff did not report any concerns about discrimination.

Staff were able to apply to work flexibly to account for personal circumstances, such as caring responsibilities or studies. Managers put reasonable adjustments in place for staff if needed.

The staff survey monitored if staff felt that they were treated equally and fairly irrespective of protected characteristics. The provider promoted inclusion networks that staff could join.
